title: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal
goal: By the end you can remove shared mutable state instead of locking it: build deeply immutable objects, publish snapshots, keep state confined to one thread, hand objects over through a queue, and use `ThreadLocal` without leaking between requests.

warmup.q: `record Quote(String pair, List<BigDecimal> tiers) {}`. A caller builds it from an `ArrayList`, then adds an element to that same `ArrayList`. What does `quote.tiers()` show?
options: The original elements: records are immutable
The new element too: the record holds the caller's list
It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when the caller adds
It depends on whether the record was built with `new`
warmup.why: A record's fields are final, so `tiers` will always point to the same list. But it's the caller's list, and nothing stops the caller from changing it. Records are shallowly immutable. To make the quote really immutable, copy the list in a compact constructor with `List.copyOf`.

sections.h: Records and data classes are only shallowly immutable

try.title: Mutate a record from outside
steps: Read `ShallowRecord`. `ShallowQuote` keeps the caller's list and array; `DeepQuote` copies them in and out. A third reference is an `unmodifiableList` view.
After construction, the caller changes its list and array, and a reader writes into the array it got from `signature()`. Predict all three lines.
Run it, then run the Kotlin twin, which adds one more line.

code.title: ShallowRecord.java

alt.title: ShallowRecord.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.concurrency.l11

// A data class's vals can't be reassigned. The objects they point to can still change.
private data class LooseQuote(val pair: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray)

private class SealedQuote(val pair: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) {
    val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers)    // copy in: unmodifiable even through a cast
    private val sig = signature.copyOf()
    val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf()             // copy out
}

fun main() {
    val tiers = mutableListOf("up to 10k at 1.0842")
    val sig = byteArrayOf(7, 7, 7)
    val loose = LooseQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig)              // List<String> is read-only, not immutable
    val sealed = SealedQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig)
    val view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers)  // a read-only VIEW, not a copy

    tiers.add("above 10k at 9.9999")                          // the caller keeps changing its list...
    sig[0] = 0                                                // ...and its array
    loose.signature[1] = 0                                    // a reader scribbles on what it was given
    sealed.signature[1] = 0

    println("shallow: ${loose.tiers}  signature ${loose.signature.contentToString()}")
    println("deep:    ${sealed.tiers}  signature ${sealed.signature.contentToString()}")
    println("unmodifiableList view: $view")
    (loose.tiers as MutableList<String>).add("added through a cast")   // read-only interface, mutable object
    println("shallow after a cast:  ${loose.tiers}")
}

try.expect: The shallow quote shows the extra tier and a signature of `[0, 0, 7]`: both the caller and a reader changed it. The deep quote still shows one tier and `[7, 7, 7]`. The `unmodifiableList` view shows the extra tier, because it's a view. In Kotlin, a cast to `MutableList` adds to the shallow quote's "read-only" list.

sections.h: Confinement keeps mutable state on one thread
sections.body:
Mutable state is fine as long as only one thread can reach it. That is **confinement**, and you already use it every day.

Stack confinement is the simplest: local variables live on one thread's stack. A `StringBuilder` or `ArrayList` created inside a method and never stored anywhere else needs no protection at all.

```java
String statementLine(Payment p) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();      // local: no other thread can ever see it
    sb.append(p.id()).append(';').append(p.cents());
    return sb.toString();                        // only the immutable String leaves
}
```

```kotlin
fun statementLine(p: Payment): String = buildString {   // the builder is local: no other thread can see it
    append(p.id).append(';').append(p.cents)
}                                                        // only the immutable String leaves
```

Thread confinement is the same idea at a larger scale: one thread owns some state, and every other thread asks that thread to act on it. A Kafka consumer is the classic case. Each partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state such as the last processed offset or a running total can live in a plain `HashMap` that only that thread touches. Event loops work the same way.

When work moves between threads, move ownership with it. A request thread builds a batch, puts it into a `BlockingQueue`, and never touches it again. The writer thread takes it and owns it from then on.

```java
List<Entry> batch = new ArrayList<>();          // owned by this thread
fill(batch);
queue.put(batch);                               // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, this thread never touches batch again
```

```kotlin
val batch = ArrayList<Entry>()                  // owned by this thread
fill(batch)
queue.put(batch)                                // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, this thread never touches batch again
```

The queue does two jobs. It hands the object over, and it makes the hand-off visible: everything the producer did before `put` happens-before the consumer's `take` returns. The figure shows the moment ownership changes. The rule is all on the producer: once you've handed it over, it isn't yours. A producer that reuses the list for the next batch is sharing a mutable object with no synchronization at all, and the writer sees half-cleared batches.

try.title: Hand over, or keep using?
steps: Read `HandOff`. A producer fills 5,000 batches of 100 entries and puts each into a queue. A writer thread checks that every batch it takes is complete and in order.
Run it. Then run it with `-Pargs=reuse`, where the producer clears and refills one list instead of creating a new one.
Run the `reuse` version a few times. Is the damage count the same each time?

sections.h: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy, and pools keep it forever

try.title: Watch one customer's context leak into another's request
steps: Read `ThreadLocalBleed`. Six requests run one after another on a pool of one thread. The handler sets the user only when the request carries one.
Predict what each request without a user runs as, in the leaky version and in the clean one.

code.title: ThreadLocalBleed.java

alt.title: ThreadLocalBleed.kt

try.expect: Leaky: the first anonymous request runs as `alice`, and the next two run as `bob`, whoever that thread served last. Clean: every anonymous request runs as `null`, because `remove()` in `finally` put the thread back as it was. A pool of one makes it happen every time. With 200 threads it happens rarely and randomly, which is how it reaches production.

analogy: An immutable object is a printed price list: anyone can read it at the same time, and to change a price you print a new list and swap it on the wall. Confinement is a ledger kept in one clerk's desk; others pass notes to that clerk instead of writing in it. A hand-off through a queue is passing a folder across the counter: once it's handed over, you don't reach back to add a page. A `ThreadLocal` on a pool thread is a locker that the next shift inherits, with whatever the last person left in it, unless someone empties it at the end of every shift. The analogy breaks at the price list: a printed list can't be edited by a stranger, but a Java object with one unprotected `List` field can.
in_your_world: Kafka already confines state for you: one partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state needs no locks, as long as you don't hand it to another thread. Events and commands on the bus should be immutable records, so a consumer can pass them to a worker pool without copying. Temporal runs a workflow's code one thread at a time, so workflow state is confined by design; activities run on an ordinary thread pool and get none of that protection. And look at every `ThreadLocal` in your Quarkus services, including the ones inside libraries: logging MDC, a tenant or merchant context, a security principal. Each one needs a `finally` that clears it, or a framework hook that does it for you. A merchant id that leaks from one request into the next is a reportable incident, not just a bug.
mistake: The most common mistake is setting a `ThreadLocal` and never clearing it, usually because the code was written and tested where each request seemed to get a fresh thread. On a pool, the value stays on the thread. The next request that doesn't set it reads the previous request's tenant, user or MDC fields, and the logs show one customer's id on another customer's payment. Unit tests rarely catch it, because each test usually runs on a fresh thread or in a fresh JVM. The fix is mechanical: every `set` is paired with a `remove()` in a `finally`, or replaced by a scoped value on JDK 25 and later. The lab's `TenantScope` goes one step further and restores the previous value, so nested calls work too.

compare.title: A deeply immutable value in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java record

kotlin.title: Kotlin class

compare.note: Both compile to a class with `final` fields, so both get the memory model's final-field guarantee. The difference is where the copy can go. A Java record's compact constructor may reassign its parameters before the fields are set, so `payments = List.copyOf(payments)` stores the copy. A Kotlin data class can't do that, because its primary-constructor parameters are the properties, so you use a plain class with a separate property, as here, or a private constructor and a factory. Kotlin's `List` type doesn't help as much as it looks: it's a read-only interface, and `listOf` or `toList` results can still be changed through a cast or from Java. `java.util.List.copyOf` gives you a list that is unmodifiable for everyone. Data class `copy()` is shallow too: the copy shares the same list.

worked.title: A shared constant that someone changed

steps.say: A payment service adds a card fee to every order. `Money` looks like a value, and `CARD_FEE` looks like a constant. Read it and find what changes, and for whom.

`add` changes the object it's called on. The line `order.amount().add(CARD_FEE)` changes the order's own amount. Somewhere else, `CARD_FEE.add(surcharge)` changes the fee for every request on every thread. And because `cents` is neither `final` nor `volatile`, other threads may see the old fee, the new one, or a mix, at different times. `static final` on the reference didn't make the object constant.
Make `Money` a value: final fields, and operations that return a new instance. Now `CARD_FEE` can be read by 200 threads with no lock, and nobody can change it.

Before reading on, explain to yourself why the record version needs no synchronization even though `CARD_FEE` is read by every request thread. Then look at the classic trap with immutable types, which catches people moving from mutable ones: calling the operation and ignoring the result.
steps.alt_code:
var total = BigDecimal.ZERO
for (fee in fees) total.add(fee)                 // does nothing: the result is thrown away
for (fee in fees) total += fee                   // right: plus() returns a new BigDecimal

steps.say: Answer: the fields are `final`, set once in the constructor, and the object never changes, so every thread that can see the reference sees 30 EUR. There is nothing to race on. The price is an allocation per operation, which the JIT often removes when the object doesn't escape. For money, that trade is easy.

lab.title: A deeply immutable quote and a tenant scope that cleans up
steps: Run the tests. All six fail. The three `FxQuote` tests change the quote from outside, through the list you passed in, the list it returns, and its signature array. The three `TenantScope` tests run on a pool of one thread and find a tenant left over from an earlier call.
Give `FxQuote` a compact constructor that replaces `tiers` with `List.copyOf(tiers)` and `signature` with a clone.
Override `signature()` so it returns a clone, not the field.

Fix `TenantScope.runAs`: remember the previous value, set the new one (or `remove()` for `null`), run the work in a `try`, and in `finally` put the previous value back (or `remove()` if there was none).
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: In a compact constructor you assign to the parameter (`tiers = List.copyOf(tiers);`), not to `this.tiers`. The record assigns the fields after your code runs.
`List.copyOf` also rejects `null` elements, which is usually what you want in a quote.
Restoring the previous value instead of always calling `remove()` makes nested calls work: an inner `runAs` must hand the thread back to the outer one, not wipe it.

drill.title: An immutable refund from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an immutable `Refund` with a payment id, a list of line items and a reason, safe to share between threads, plus `withReason(String)` that returns a changed copy. Check: can the caller's list, or the list you return, change your refund?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: An object nobody can change needs no locks. Make fields final, add no setters, copy mutable parts, and don't let `this` escape.
For data that changes now and then, publish an immutable snapshot through a `volatile` field and replace it whole.
Records and data classes are shallow. Copy lists with `List.copyOf` and clone arrays in and out. `unmodifiableList` is a view, not a copy.
Confinement: locals, one owner thread (one Kafka partition per consumer), or ownership handed through a queue and never touched again.
Every `ThreadLocal.set` on a pool thread needs a `remove()` in `finally`. On JDK 25+, scoped values do the cleanup for you.

quiz.q: Which of these can be shared between threads with no synchronization at all?
options: A record whose `List<String>` component is the caller's `ArrayList`
A class with `volatile` fields and setters
A final class whose `private final` fields are a `String`, an `Instant` and a `BigDecimal`, with no setters
A record with an `int[]` component and the default accessor
quiz.why: All three field types are immutable and the fields are final, so the object can never change and the final-field rule makes it visible correctly. The record with the caller's list and the record with an array can be changed from outside. `volatile` fields with setters make each write visible, but the object still changes under readers.

quiz.q: A constructor stores `this.items = Collections.unmodifiableList(items);`. The caller later adds an item to its own `items` list. What does the object's list show?
options: The original items only
It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` in the caller
The caller's add is ignored
The new item too, because `unmodifiableList` is a view of the caller's list
quiz.why: `unmodifiableList` only stops *you* from changing the list through that reference. It still reads the caller's list, so the caller's changes show through. `List.copyOf` makes a copy that nobody can change.

quiz.q: From explicit locks: an FX rate table is replaced as a whole every 5 seconds and read 5,000 times a second. What is the simplest correct design?
options: A `ReentrantReadWriteLock` around a `HashMap`
A `volatile` field holding an immutable map, replaced with a freshly built `Map.copyOf(...)` on each refresh
A `ConcurrentHashMap` refreshed with `clear()` and `putAll()`
A `synchronized` getter and setter on a `HashMap`
quiz.why: Readers never block, and each one sees one complete version, because the new map is built fully before one `volatile` write publishes it. The read-write lock also works, with more code and some cost on every read. `clear` plus `putAll` on a concurrent map lets readers see an empty or half-filled table.

quiz.q: A Quarkus request handler does `USER.set(request.user())` on a `ThreadLocal` when the request is authenticated, and never removes it. What does a later anonymous request on the same worker thread see?
options: The previous request's user
`null`, because each request gets a fresh thread
An `IllegalStateException`
A random user from another thread
quiz.why: Worker threads come from a pool and are reused. The value stays on the thread until someone removes it, so the anonymous request runs as whoever that thread served last. Pair every `set` with `remove()` in `finally`.

quiz.q: A producer puts an `ArrayList` of entries into a `BlockingQueue`, then calls `clear()` on the same list and refills it for the next batch. What does that do to the consumer?
options: Nothing: `take()` returns a copy of the list
Nothing: `put` made the list thread-safe
The consumer can see a partly cleared or refilled batch, because the producer kept changing an object it had handed over
`put` throws, because the list is already in the queue
quiz.why: The queue hands over a reference, not a copy. `put` happens-before `take` only for what the producer did before the `put`. After that, the producer and consumer share one mutable list with no synchronization. Hand over a new list each time.

flashcards.front: What does a class need to be immutable?
flashcards.back: All fields `final` and set in the constructor, no setters, mutable components copied in and never handed out, and `this` doesn't escape during construction.

flashcards.front: What does the memory model guarantee for `final` fields?
flashcards.back: A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even without synchronization.

flashcards.front: Is a record with a `List` component immutable?
flashcards.back: Only shallowly. Copy it in the compact constructor: `items = List.copyOf(items);`.
`unmodifiableList` is a read-only view: the owner's later changes show through. `List.copyOf` is an unmodifiable copy that nobody can change.

flashcards.front: How do you share data that changes rarely, without locks?
flashcards.back: Build a new immutable snapshot, then publish it with one write to a `volatile` field (or an `AtomicReference`). Readers read the reference once.

flashcards.front: A pool thread runs a task that calls `ThreadLocal.set` and never `remove()`. What happens next?
flashcards.back: The value stays on the thread. The next task on that thread sees it if it doesn't set its own.

flashcards.front: What makes passing a mutable object through a `BlockingQueue` safe?
flashcards.back: `put` happens-before `take`, so the consumer sees everything done before the put, as long as the producer never touches the object again.

terms.plain: An object whose state can't change after construction; safe to share without locks.
Copying a mutable argument or return value so no one else can change your object through it.
Final references to objects that can still change, as in a record holding an `ArrayList`.
Replacing a whole immutable object through one `volatile` write, so readers see one complete version.
Keeping mutable state reachable by only one thread.
Passing an object to another thread, through a queue, and never touching it again.
A variable with a separate value per thread; values live as long as the thread unless removed.
A JDK 25 value bound for one call and its callees, gone when the call returns (JEP 506).

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to add a lock around a merchant-settings object that a refresher updates every minute and every request reads. Explain the alternative you'd suggest, and why it is safe.
explain_back.answer: I'd make the settings an immutable record, with final fields and copied lists, and keep the current one in a `volatile` field. The refresher builds a complete new settings object off to the side and then assigns it to the field in one write. Requests read the field once and use that object. It's safe because nothing a reader can reach is ever modified: the old object stays valid for whoever is still using it, and the `volatile` write makes the new object, including all its fields, visible to every reader that reads the field afterwards. Readers never wait, and there's no lock to forget. The one thing to watch is a reader that reads the field twice and gets two different versions, so read it into a local first.

deeper.body:
Each `Thread` object has its own small hash map for its thread locals, called `ThreadLocalMap`. The keys are weak references to the `ThreadLocal` objects, and the values are strong references. When a `ThreadLocal` itself becomes garbage, its key goes away, but the value stays in the map until a later `get`, `set` or `remove` on that thread happens to clean it up. On a pool thread that lives for days, that can be a long time. In application servers this is a famous leak: a value whose class came from a redeployed web application keeps that application's whole class loader alive. `remove()` avoids all of it.

`InheritableThreadLocal` copies values from a parent thread to a child thread when the child is created. It does nothing useful with pools, because pool threads are created once, long before the request that submits work to them.

Scoped values (JEP 506, final in JDK 25) fix the design problems rather than the symptoms. A binding is immutable: there is no `set`, so code deep in the call stack can't change the tenant under you. It has a clear lifetime: it ends when `run` or `call` returns, even on an exception. And it is cheap to share with child tasks: with structured concurrency, still a preview API in JDK 25, threads forked inside the scope see the same bindings without copying a map per thread.

One immutability trap to know: an object is only safe to share through a data race if `this` didn't escape while the constructor was running. A constructor that registers `this` as a listener, or starts a thread that uses `this`, hands out the object before its final fields are guaranteed to be visible. Build first, register after. The memory model track's lesson on safe publication covers the full rules.
